nameStory: This graceful raptor gets its name from its deeply forked tail that looks remarkably similar to a barn swallow's distinctive tail shape. The scientific name 'forficatus' comes from the Latin word for scissors, referring to the way those long tail feathers open and close like scissor blades as the bird maneuvers through the air.
description: The Swallow-tailed Kite is one of North America's most elegant raptors, with brilliant white head and body contrasting sharply with jet-black wings and that famous deeply forked black tail. These graceful birds have a wingspan of about 4 feet and appear almost tern-like in flight with their buoyant, effortless soaring style. They're specialized hunters that rarely flap their wings, instead riding air currents with remarkable skill while snatching prey from treetops or even catching insects and small animals in mid-air with their talons.

idTips.label: Deeply forked tail
idTips.description: The tail is split into two long, streaming black ribbons that constantly open and close like scissors as the bird steers through the air

idTips.label: Black and white pattern
idTips.description: Brilliant white head, neck, chest, and belly create a stark contrast with completely black wings and tail - no other large bird of prey has this clean two-toned look

idTips.label: Effortless flight style
idTips.description: Soars with wings held flat (not in a V-shape) and rarely flaps, appearing to float on air currents with incredible grace and control

idTips.label: Size and proportions
idTips.description: Appears large in flight with long, narrow wings spanning about 4 feet, but the body is relatively small and lightweight compared to other raptors

idTips.label: Feeding behavior
idTips.description: Often seen plucking prey from treetops or catching insects in flight without landing, using their feet like hands to eat while soaring

habitat: In New England, Swallow-tailed Kites are extremely rare vagrants that occasionally appear during migration, typically seen over open areas near wetlands, large rivers, or coastal zones. When spotted, they're usually soaring high over mixed forests adjacent to water sources where flying insects are abundant.

seasonality.spring: Very rare vagrant during spring migration (April-May), occasionally spotted soaring high over river valleys or coastal areas as birds overshoot their normal southeastern breeding range.
seasonality.summer: Exceptionally rare summer visitor, with most New England sightings occurring in late summer (July-August) when young birds may wander north of their typical range.
seasonality.fall: Slightly more likely during fall migration (August-September) when birds head south to wintering grounds, though still extremely uncommon in the region.
seasonality.winter: Not present - all North American birds migrate to South America for winter, making any winter sighting in New England highly unlikely.

funFact: Swallow-tailed Kites drink water by skimming the surface with their beaks while flying at full speed, never needing to land at water sources - they're so perfectly adapted to life in the air that they even mate while soaring together through the sky!
confusionNotes: The deeply forked tail and stark black-and-white pattern make this bird virtually unmistakable - no other raptor in New England has this combination of features. The closest confusion might be with a distant gull, but the pointed wings, soaring flight style, and overall size quickly eliminate that possibility.
contextualKnowledge: While called a 'kite,' this bird is actually a specialized raptor in the hawk and eagle family. The name 'kite' for certain raptors comes from their soaring flight style that resembles a toy kite dancing on air currents, not from any relationship to the paper toys we fly.
compareHints: As the only species in its genus, the Swallow-tailed Kite is compared best to other kites in the hawk family. Unlike the broader-winged Mississippi Kite that occasionally reaches New England, the Swallow-tailed Kite has that unmistakable forked tail, bright white underparts, and much more contrasting plumage pattern. It's significantly more graceful in flight than any other North American raptor.
